subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Cells and Organisms
subtitle: Cell structures, life processes, plant and animal cells, unicellular and multicellular organisms, and evidence from investigations.
description: A source-faithful life science pack about how cells work together to keep organisms alive. Students practise key cell structures, cell theory, plant and animal cell comparison, levels of organization, matter and energy, homeostasis, diffusion, microscopes, and yeast investigation evidence.

data.targetWord: the smallest unit of life that can carry out life processes

examples.en-US: A cell is the smallest unit of life that can carry out life processes.

data.targetWord: any living thing

examples.en-US: An organism is any living thing, whether it is one cell or many cells.

data.targetWord: an organism made of one cell

examples.en-US: A bacterium is a unicellular organism because it is made of one cell.

data.targetWord: an organism made of many cells

examples.en-US: A human is a multicellular organism because the body contains many specialized cells.

data.targetWord: a thin boundary around a cell that controls what enters and leaves

examples.en-US: A red blood cell is small and flexible so it can move through tiny blood vessels.

examples.en-US: Yeast can make bread dough rise by producing carbon dioxide gas.

examples.en-US: Diffusion moves particles from higher concentration to lower concentration.

data.title: Levels of Organization
data.instruction: Put the levels of organization in order from smallest to largest.
items: Cell
Tissue
Organ
Organ system
Organism

data.title: Photosynthesis to Energy Use
data.instruction: Put the events in order from sunlight reaching a leaf to cells using sugar.
items: Sunlight reaches chloroplasts in plant cells.
Chloroplasts use carbon dioxide and water with light energy.
Sugar and oxygen are produced during photosynthesis.
Cells use sugar as food matter.
Mitochondria help release usable energy from sugar during cellular respiration.

data.title: Yeast Temperature Investigation
data.instruction: Put the investigation steps in a sensible order.
items: Prepare bottles with the same amount of yeast, sugar, and water.
Change only the water temperature for each bottle.
Place a balloon over each bottle opening.
Wait the same amount of time for every bottle.
Measure balloon circumference as evidence of carbon dioxide production.
Compare the measurements to decide which temperature produced the most yeast activity.

data.title: Using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning
data.instruction: Put the parts of a strong science response in order.
items: State a clear claim that answers the question.
Choose specific evidence from data, observations, or facts.
Explain how the evidence supports the claim using science ideas.
Avoid claiming more than the evidence supports.
